annotations.text:
CLICKABLE — tap through the whole turn: bet → sign → answer → reveal. "Restart" resets it.

Use the DOMAIN chip above the frame to switch between the five sign types. Each one is a different physical object with its own item, its own question, its own component breakdown and its own confusable — not the same card recoloured.

  transit   出口   the exit plate
  menu      辣     the spicy marker in a menu section
  street    药店   a shopfront fascia
  market    斤     the 500g trap on a price label
  safety    小心地滑  a hazard board

The TONE COLOUR chip turns tone colouring on and off. It sits on the pinyin, never on the character.

The bet is how much scaffolding you give up:
  +1 / −1    pinyin shown, answers in English
  +5 / −3    no pinyin
  +15 / −10  no pinyin, and the four answers are signs too

Pick "Cold read" on any domain to see the four-hanzi variant — the distractors are real signs you would plausibly confuse it with, which is where most of the teaching happens.

The five treatments side by side.

Each caption says what the object is and what makes it hard — the shopfront is deliberately the least legible, the price label deliberately buries the character under the price, because those are the real reading conditions.

What this costs: five sign templates to build and maintain instead of one, and every new category needs a treatment designed for it rather than a colour picked for it. That is the trade. I think it is worth it — the object is a retrieval cue, and learning 斤 on a price label is closer to the real task than learning it on a neutral card.

Still open, pending the research sweep: whether tone colour survives the evidence, and whether the gloss should be Dutch or English (both are shown for now).
